name: Local Models for Patient Data
title: Local Models for Patient Data
answer: Local models for patient data are AI systems that process protected health information entirely within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, rather than sending it to external cloud services. This includes models embedded in medical devices, on-premises servers, and edge devices used for diagnosis, triage, documentation, or monitoring. The scope covers governance, compliance, and medical device security questions that arise when a model touches identifiable patient records. It also includes the operational boundaries between local inference, remote updates, and vendor support.

sections.body: Local models for patient data are AI systems that process protected health information entirely within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, rather than sending it to external cloud services. This includes models embedded in medical devices, on-premises servers, and edge devices used for diagnosis, triage, documentation, or monitoring. The scope covers governance, compliance, and medical device security questions that arise when a model touches identifiable patient records. It also includes the operational boundaries between local inference, remote updates, and vendor support.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These models run on hospital-owned servers, dedicated GPU workstations, private cloud clusters, or embedded accelerators inside medical devices. They require local model registries, container runtimes, and inference engines that can operate without continuous internet access. Many deployments use air-gapped networks or strict egress controls so that patient data never leaves the clinical environment. Hardware must meet availability and latency requirements for real-time clinical use, and often includes redundant power and encrypted storage.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by downloading or training model weights inside the organization, then running inference locally on patient data. Clinical teams validate the model against local patient cohorts to check for performance drift and demographic fit before use. Data engineers maintain versioned model artifacts, feature pipelines, and audit logs that record every inference request and output. Fine-tuning on local data is common, but it must be done with de-identified or properly consented records and under change control.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Local deployment reduces third-party data exposure but does not remove obligations under HIPAA, GDPR, or medical device regulations such as the EU MDR and FDA guidance. Organizations must still document model provenance, training data lineage, and the basis for any clinical claim. Patient rights to access, correction, and deletion apply to locally stored inputs and outputs, and audit trails must show who ran which model on whose data. Security risks include insider access, unpatched local software, and model theft, while liability for incorrect outputs remains with the deploying institution or device manufacturer. The site's tracking of six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies shows that local hosting does not by itself resolve accountability.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Local models are moving toward smaller, more efficient architectures that can run on hospital-owned hardware and embedded medical devices without cloud round trips. Federated learning and confidential computing are likely to let organizations train or update models across sites while keeping raw patient data local. Regulators are expected to clarify how local deployment affects medical device classification, post-market surveillance, and software update obligations. The direction is toward auditable, on-premises AI that can meet both clinical performance and data residency requirements.
